summary: Defines how to use a JSON Web Token (JWT) as a bearer credential with OAuth 2.0, either to request an access token or to authenticate a client. It is a profile of the assertion framework in RFC 7521 and is widely used for service-to-service authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: OAuth 2.0 is the framework where an application gets permission to act for a user. This RFC describes how to use a JSON Web Token, a signed piece of JSON, for two jobs: asking for an access token, and proving that the client asking is who it says it is. It says exactly which claims the token must carry and what the server must check before believing it.

questions: what is the jwt bearer grant type
how does jwt client authentication work in oauth
which claims are required in an oauth jwt assertion
subtitle: How a signed JSON token can ask for an access token or stand in for a client's password.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 has a general framework for using a security token as an authorization grant or as client credentials, but that framework does not say what such a token must contain when it is a JSON Web Token.
tldr.mechanism: This profile defines two ways to send a JSON Web Token (JWT) to a token endpoint: as an authorization grant in an assertion parameter with a grant type of urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer, and as client authentication in a client_assertion parameter with a client assertion type of urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer. It then lists the claims the server must check and the rules it must enforce.
tldr.outcome: An authorization server now has one fixed list of validation rules to apply to every JWT it is sent, and one error code for each way the token can be wrong. Replay protection is left optional, and the RFC states that tokens carrying personal information should travel over an encrypted channel.

today: RFC 7523 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a profile of the assertion framework in RFC 7521 and builds on the JSON Web Token defined in RFC 7519 and the OAuth framework in RFC 6749.

sections.title: What This Profile Adds to OAuth
sections.content:
A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a JSON-based security token that lets identity and security information be shared across security domains. A security token is generally issued by an Identity Provider and consumed by a Relying Party that relies on its content to identify the token's subject. OAuth 2.0 provides a method for making authenticated HTTP requests to a resource using an access token, and it allows new grant types and new client authentication mechanisms to be defined as extensions.

RFC 7521 is an abstract extension to OAuth 2.0 that gives a general framework for using assertions, also called security tokens, as client credentials and authorization grants. This specification profiles that framework for one kind of token, the JWT. It defines an extension grant type that uses a JWT Bearer Token to request an OAuth 2.0 access token, and it defines how a JWT can be used to authenticate the client.

The two uses are separate from each other. Using a JWT to authenticate the client is just another way for a client to prove who it is at the token endpoint, and it has to be used together with some grant type to make a complete request. A JWT authorization grant may be used with or without client authentication. Whether client authentication is needed, and which kinds are accepted, are policy decisions for the authorization server. How the client obtains the JWT in the first place is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC says how to use a signed piece of JSON, called a JSON Web Token, in two places in OAuth: as the ticket that asks for an access token, and as the proof that the applicant is the client it says it is. It also lists the exact checks a server must make before it trusts such a token.

sections.title: Sending a JWT to Get an Access Token
sections.content:
To use a Bearer JWT as an authorization grant, the client sends an access token request as defined in Section 4 of the OAuth Assertion Framework, with three specific parameter values. The value of grant_type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer. The value of the assertion parameter MUST contain a single JWT. The scope parameter may be used to indicate the requested scope. Authentication of the client is optional, so client_id is only needed when a form of client authentication that relies on that parameter is used.

The RFC shows the request as a form post to a token endpoint. The grant type and the assertion are ordinary form fields, with the JWT carried in the assertion field.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends the JWT to the token endpoint in a form field called assertion, and names the kind of request it is with a grant type of urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer. The server then checks the JWT against a fixed list of rules before it issues an access token.

sections.title: Using a JWT to Prove the Client's Identity
sections.content:
To use a JWT Bearer Token for client authentication, the client sends the same kind of request with two different parameter values. The value of client_assertion_type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer. The value of the client_assertion parameter contains a single JWT, and it MUST NOT contain more than one JWT.

The RFC's example shows this combined with an authorization code grant: the client sends the code and the client assertion in one access token request, so the request both returns the access token for the code and authenticates the client that is asking for it.
sections.plainLanguage: The same kind of token can also stand in for a client's password. The client puts the JWT in a field called client_assertion and names the type of assertion it is, so the server knows it must check the token against the client it belongs to.

sections.title: What the Server Must Check in the JWT
sections.content:
Before it issues an access token or relies on a JWT for client authentication, the authorization server MUST validate the JWT against the criteria in this section. Further restrictions and policy are at the discretion of the server.

Four claims are required. The iss claim holds a unique identifier for the entity that issued the JWT, and unless an application profile says otherwise, issuer values MUST be compared using the Simple String Comparison method of RFC 3986. The sub claim identifies the principal the JWT is about. For an authorization grant it typically identifies the resource owner or an authorised delegate, and sometimes a pseudonymous identifier or another value denoting an anonymous user; for client authentication it MUST be the client_id of the OAuth client. The aud claim identifies the authorization server as an intended audience, and the server MUST reject any JWT that does not contain its own identity as the intended audience. The exp claim limits the window during which the JWT can be used, and the server MUST reject a JWT whose expiration time has passed, subject to allowable clock skew between systems.

Three further claims are optional. The nbf claim identifies the time before which the token must not be accepted. The iat claim identifies the time at which the JWT was issued. The jti claim gives the token a unique identifier, and the server MAY keep the set of used values so that a JWT is not replayed. A JWT MAY contain other claims. It MUST be digitally signed or have a Message Authentication Code (MAC) applied by the issuer, and the server MUST reject JWTs with an invalid signature or MAC. The server MUST also reject a JWT that is not valid in all other respects under the JWT specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks four things in every token: who issued it, who it is about, which server it was meant for, and when it stops being usable. Three more claims are useful but optional: a not-before time, an issue time, and a unique id. The token must also carry a signature or a MAC, and the server rejects the token if that does not check out.

sections.title: What the Server Returns When Something Fails
sections.content:
JWT authorization grants may be used with or without client authentication or identification. If client credentials are present in the request, the authorization server MUST validate them.

If the JWT is not valid, or the current time is not inside the token's valid window, the server builds an error response as defined in OAuth 2.0. The value of the error parameter MUST be invalid_grant. The server MAY add the reason using the error_description or error_uri parameters; the RFC's example returns a bad request with a description saying that audience validation failed.

If the client JWT is not valid, the server builds an error response in the same way, but the value of the error parameter MUST be invalid_client, again with an optional description or URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Two error codes tell the client what went wrong. A bad token in the grant field gives invalid_grant, and a bad token in the client authentication field gives invalid_client. Both can carry a short description of the reason.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC builds a JWT issued and signed by the system entity identified as https://jwt-idp.example.com, with a subject identified by email address as mike@example.com, and an intended audience of https://jwt-rp.example.net, which is the identifier the authorization server uses for itself. The JWT is sent to the token endpoint at https://authz.example.net/token.oauth2.

The claims set is a JSON object holding the issuer, the subject, the audience, a not-before time of 1300815780, an expiry of 1300819380 and one extra claim, http://claims.example.com/member, set to true. The header is {"alg":"ES256","kid":"16"}, which declares that the token is signed with the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) P-256 SHA-256 using a key identified by the kid value 16.

The client then presents that token in an HTTPS request to the token endpoint, with the grant type in the grant_type field and the token in the assertion field.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC shows a complete example: a token whose issuer is one organisation, whose subject is a person's email address, and whose audience is the server that will receive it. The header names the signing algorithm and the key. The client then posts the token to the token endpoint.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations described in the OAuth Assertion Framework, in the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework and in the JWT specification all apply to this document.

The specification does not mandate replay protection for the JWT used either as an authorization grant or for client authentication. It is an optional feature, which implementations may employ at their own discretion. The claims that make replay protection possible are the exp claim, which limits how long a token may be used, and the jti claim, whose used values a server may keep for as long as the token would still be valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is explicit about one thing: it does not require servers to stop a token being used twice. A server that wants that protection has to keep track of the token ids itself, and can use the expiry time to know how long to keep them.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
A JWT may contain privacy-sensitive information, and to prevent disclosure of such information to unintended parties it should only be transmitted over encrypted channels such as Transport Layer Security (TLS). Where it is desirable to prevent disclosure of certain information to the client, the JWT should be encrypted to the authorization server.

Deployments should determine the minimum amount of information necessary to complete the exchange and include only such claims in the JWT. In some cases the sub claim can be a value representing an anonymous or pseudonymous user, as described in Section 6.3.1 of the OAuth Assertion Framework.
sections.plainLanguage: A token can carry personal information, so it should travel over an encrypted connection, and it should be encrypted to the server when even the client should not see what is inside. The rule for what goes in is simple: only what the exchange actually needs.

viz.caption: THE TWO WAYS A JWT REACHES THE TOKEN ENDPOINT

messages.label: ACCESS TOKEN REQUEST
messages.note: grant_type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer and assertion holds a single JWT.

messages.label: ACCESS TOKEN
messages.note: Sent after the JWT passes every validation rule.

messages.label: TOKEN REQUEST WITH CLIENT ASSERTION
messages.note: client_assertion_type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer and client_assertion holds a single JWT, sent with some grant type.

messages.label: ERROR RESPONSE
messages.note: invalid_client if the client assertion fails, invalid_grant if the grant assertion fails.

viz.caption: THE CLAIMS AN AUTHORIZATION SERVER CHECKS

items.title: iss, required
items.text: Issuer. Names the entity that issued the JWT.

items.title: sub, required
items.text: Subject. Names the principal the JWT is about.

items.title: aud, required
items.text: Audience. Names the authorization server as an intended audience. A token meant for another server must be rejected.

items.title: exp, required
items.text: Expiration time. Limits the window in which the JWT can be used.

items.title: nbf, optional
items.text: Not before. The time before which the token must not be accepted.

items.title: iat, optional
items.text: Issued at. The time at which the JWT was issued.

items.title: jti, optional
items.text: JWT ID. A unique identifier the server can use to detect replay.
